passage:
In Trisha's village, the little goat Chutki had followed her everywhere, even to the school gate. Then one cold morning Chutki wouldn't get up, and by evening she was gone.
Trisha sat behind the cowshed for hours. "I should have covered her with the old shawl last night," she kept thinking. "I should have checked on her. It's my fault."
Her uncle Kishore found her there. He looked after the village animals and had seen Chutki the day before. He crouched beside her. "Trisha, Chutki had a sickness inside. Even I couldn't see it. A shawl wouldn't have changed anything."
"But I didn't check."
"You fed her, played with her, carried her across the stream. She had a very loved life."
Trisha leaned on his shoulder and finally cried properly.

qa.q: Where did Chutki follow Trisha?
qa.a: Everywhere, even to the school gate.

qa.q: Why did Trisha keep thinking it was her fault?
qa.a: She felt guilty, believing that a shawl or checking on Chutki could have saved her.

qa.q: What did Kishore say that helped Trisha?
qa.a: He explained that Chutki had a hidden sickness nobody could see, and reminded Trisha how well she had loved Chutki.

qa.q: How does Kishore see Trisha's guilt?
qa.a: He sees a child wrongly blaming herself, so he gently corrects her with facts and with her own kindness.

grounding: A girl blames herself for her pet goat's death until a trusted adult helps her see it was not her fault and that she loved it well.

passage:
In their apartment in Amman, Nour's canary, Limoon, had sung every morning since before she could read. On Friday he was lying still at the bottom of his cage.
Nour wouldn't touch her breakfast. "Last week I forgot to change his water one day," she whispered. "Maybe that's why. Maybe I killed him."
Her aunt Rania put down the coffee pot and sat beside her. "Habibti, look at me. Limoon was very old for a canary. Birds his age just stop one day. One day of old water did not do this."
"Are you sure?"
"I'm sure. Who cleaned his cage every Saturday? Who sang back to him?"
Nour sniffed. "Me."
"Then he had a good life because of you." Nour put her head in her aunt's lap and cried until her chest felt looser.

qa.q: What did Nour say she forgot to do last week?
qa.a: To change Limoon's water one day.

qa.q: Why wouldn't Nour touch her breakfast?
qa.a: She felt guilty and frightened, believing she had killed Limoon.

qa.q: How did Rania help Nour see things differently?
qa.a: She explained that Limoon was very old and reminded Nour of all the care she had given him.

qa.q: How might Rania have felt hearing Nour say "Maybe I killed him"?
qa.a: Probably sad and concerned, wanting to lift that wrong blame from Nour straight away.

grounding: A girl blames herself for her canary's death, and talking with an adult helps her see it was not her fault and that she cared for it well.

passage:
Babysitter's note for Mrs. Rao, Wednesday evening
You asked me to write down how the children were today. When Seema and Jagdish found Mitthu still in his cage after school, Jagdish sobbed so hard he hiccuped. Seema's own eyes were red, but she sat on the floor, pulled her little brother close and said, "Let's say goodbye to Mitthu properly." She helped him draw a parrot with a crown. Halfway through, she cried too, and they cried together for a while. Then she read him the parrot page from his animal book.
I stayed close by, brought them water and let them be. They buried Mitthu under the neem tree with a marigold. At dinner Jagdish ate everything and asked Seema to sleep in his room. She said yes.

qa.q: What did Seema help Jagdish draw?
qa.a: A parrot with a crown.

qa.q: How was Seema feeling while she comforted Jagdish?
qa.a: She was sad herself, with red eyes, but wanted to look after her little brother; halfway through, she cried too.

qa.q: What did the babysitter do that helped?
qa.a: They stayed close, brought water and let the children grieve together.

qa.q: How did Jagdish experience Seema's comfort?
qa.a: He felt safer and closer to her, eating his dinner and asking her to sleep in his room.

grounding: A note shows a girl comforting her little brother after their parrot dies, which lets her feel her own sorrow and brings them closer.

passage:
Sunday night
Bijli died this morning. The vet said her heart was weak from the start. Bhupen is only six, and at first he didn't understand. He kept pouring milk into her saucer. Then he understood, and he screamed and cried and hid under the bed.
I wanted to hide too. But I crawled under the bed with him and said, "Remember when Bijli fell in the bucket?" He laughed a tiny bit, then cried more. So did I. We stayed under there till Maa called us for lunch.
Funny thing. Looking after Bhupen made my own crying come out. Before that it was stuck. Now I feel closer to him than ever. He's asleep on my bed right now.
Nilesh

qa.q: What did the vet say about Bijli's heart?
qa.a: It was weak from the start.

qa.q: What did Nilesh notice about Nilesh's own sadness while comforting Bhupen?
qa.a: The stuck crying finally came out, and Nilesh felt closer to Bhupen than ever.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that helped Bhupen?
qa.a: Nilesh crawled under the bed with Bhupen and shared a funny memory of Bijli.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt when Nilesh crawled under the bed?
qa.a: Less alone; he laughed a tiny bit and later fell asleep on Nilesh's bed.

grounding: A child comforting a little brother after their kitten dies finds it releases their own sorrow and brings them closer.

passage:
In the Johannesburg house, Ba's chair by the window was empty now. For two weeks Bao had kept expecting to hear her slippers and her low songs in Vietnamese. He missed her hands most, wrinkled and warm, peeling oranges for him in one long curl.
Some days he felt fine and played football with Thabo from next door. Then a smell of ginger from the kitchen would knock him sideways, and he'd run to his room.
On Saturday his mother found him crying on Ba's chair. She sat on the arm. "It comes in waves, doesn't it?"
Bao nodded. "Is it bad that I was laughing yesterday?"
"No. Laughing and crying both mean you loved her."
That evening Bao peeled an orange in one long curl, the way she had taught him, and set it by her photo.

qa.q: What did Ba do with oranges for Bao?
qa.a: She peeled them for him in one long curl.

qa.q: What happened to Bao's feelings when he smelled ginger?
qa.a: A wave of grief knocked him sideways; he missed Ba so much he ran to his room.

qa.q: How did Bao find a way to keep loving Ba?
qa.a: By letting himself cry and remember her, and by peeling an orange her way to set by her photo.

qa.q: How did Bao's mother see his worry about laughing?
qa.a: She saw laughing and crying both as signs of love, not something bad.

grounding: A boy misses his grandmother's stories and hands, feels grief in waves, and lets himself cry and remember her as a way of loving her still.

passage:
Manjula had been back at school for three days since Ajji's funeral. She had done her sums, eaten her lunch and even laughed at Deepa's joke. Then in Kannada class, Yamini Ma'am began reading a poem about a grandmother braiding jasmine into a girl's hair.
Manjula's throat closed. Ajji used to braid her hair every morning, her hands smelling of coconut oil. The words on the page blurred.
Yamini Ma'am noticed. She kept reading, but walked past and quietly set a note on the desk: "Library corner if you need it."
Manjula went. She sat on the beanbag and cried into her sleeve. After a while Ma'am came, sat beside her and said nothing, only held her hand. Later Manjula drew Ajji's hands braiding, and under it wrote, "Still here."

qa.q: What was the poem about?
qa.a: A grandmother braiding jasmine into a girl's hair.

qa.q: What made Manjula's throat close in class?
qa.a: A sudden wave of grief; the poem reminded her how much she missed Ajji braiding her hair.

qa.q: How did Yamini Ma'am support Manjula?
qa.a: She quietly offered the library corner, then sat beside her and held her hand without talking.

qa.q: What might Yamini Ma'am have noticed during the poem?
qa.a: She saw Manjula's grief rise in a wave and wanted to give her a private place to feel it.

grounding: A girl whose grandmother has died is caught by a wave of grief at school and lets herself cry and remember her.

passage: Payal, you saw your Papa crying last night and it scared you? Come here. Let your Baljeet Nani tell you something. When I was about your age, my Dadi died. On the day of the bhog, I found my father in the cattle shed, alone, crying like a small boy. I had never seen him cry, not once. I froze. My big strong Bapu! I wanted to run away. But I stood there, and then I walked in and put my arms around his waist. I said, "I miss Dadi too." He held me so tightly. After that, he told me stories about her I had never heard. Grown-ups feel things deeply too, puttar. So tonight, you go and sit with your Papa. Just hug him.

qa.q: Where did young Baljeet find her father crying?
qa.a: In the cattle shed, alone.

qa.q: How did young Baljeet feel when she saw her Bapu crying?
qa.a: Frightened and frozen; she had never seen him cry and wanted to run away.

qa.q: What choice in Nani's story made a difference?
qa.a: Walking in, hugging her Bapu and saying she missed Dadi too, which brought them closer.

qa.q: How might Bapu have felt when his daughter hugged him?
qa.a: Comforted and less alone; he held her tightly and later shared stories about his mother.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being frightened to see her father cry after a death, and how hugging him and sharing her sadness helped them both.

passage:
The power went out the evening after Ajoba's funeral, and the flat filled with guests' whispers and candle smoke. Nilesh went to the kitchen for water and stopped in the doorway. Aai stood at the dark window, shoulders shaking, crying without any sound.
He had never seen her cry. Not even when she burnt her hand on the tawa. His stomach went cold. If Aai was falling apart, who would hold everything together?
Ayesha from the flat next door, carrying a tray of cups, squeezed past him and whispered, "Go to her."
Nilesh walked over and put his arms around Aai from behind. "I'm sad too, Aai."
Aai turned and held him close. "I know, baba. I'm crying because I loved him, the same as you." In the candlelight they stood together until the lights came back on.

qa.q: What happened the evening after Ajoba's funeral?
qa.a: The power went out.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh's stomach go cold in the doorway?
qa.a: He felt frightened, having never seen Aai cry, and worried about who would hold everything together.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do that helped them both?
qa.a: He hugged Aai from behind and told her he was sad too.

qa.q: How did Aai explain her tears?
qa.a: She was crying because she loved Ajoba, the same as Nilesh, showing that adults grieve deeply too.

grounding: A boy is frightened to see his mother cry for the first time after a death, then hugs her and says he is sad too.

passage:
Forty-nine days after Grandpa died, relatives filled the small house in Osaka again. Hiroshi had dreaded it. He didn't know what to say to aunts he barely knew.
But when the monk began chanting, everyone's voices rose and fell together, and Hiroshi found his own lips moving along. Incense curled past Grandpa's photo. His cousin Lucia, visiting from Milan, whose family prayed differently at home, knelt beside him and bowed when everyone bowed.
Afterwards the aunts brought out rice balls and Grandpa's favourite pickled plums. Great-uncle Kenji told a story about Grandpa falling into a fishpond, and the whole room laughed.
Walking to the station, Hiroshi felt that the heaviness he had carried for weeks had been shared out, like the rice balls, among everyone.

qa.q: What did the aunts bring out after the chanting?
qa.a: Rice balls and Grandpa's favourite pickled plums.

qa.q: How did Hiroshi feel before the gathering, and how did that change?
qa.a: He felt dread and awkwardness at first, then comfort as the heaviness felt shared among everyone.

qa.q: What in the gathering helped the family carry their sorrow?
qa.a: Chanting together, sharing food and laughing at stories about Grandpa.

qa.q: How might Lucia have experienced the ritual?
qa.a: Although her family prays differently, she joined in respectfully and shared in the sense of belonging.

grounding: A boy dreading a memorial gathering finds that shared chanting, food and stories help the family carry sorrow together, whatever their beliefs.

passage:
The community hall smelled of marigolds and ghee. Vishal sat on the durrie at the front, beside Nani's garlanded photo, for the prayer meeting on the thirteenth day. He had expected to feel strange and on show.
Then the bhajan group began, and aunties he barely knew sang the songs Nani used to hum while cutting vegetables. Vishal knew every tune. He sang softly, and his chest ached and warmed at the same time.
His best friend Manoj came with his Ammi, both in white. They sat at the back, and when the singing ended, Manoj's Ammi hugged Vishal's mother for a long time.
Then came the food: puri, kaddu and the kheer Nani always made. Uncles served, cousins ran about. Vishal ate with Manoj on the steps, and for the first time in two weeks he felt part of something, not alone in his sadness.

qa.q: Where was the prayer meeting held?
qa.a: In the community hall.

qa.q: What did Vishal feel when he heard Nani's songs?
qa.a: His chest ached and warmed at once; he felt sad and comforted together.

qa.q: What parts of the day helped Vishal carry his grief?
qa.a: Singing Nani's familiar songs, sharing the food, and having Manoj there.

qa.q: How might Manoj's Ammi have seen the gathering?
qa.a: As a chance to comfort a grieving friend's family; she came in white and hugged Vishal's mother for a long time.

grounding: At a prayer meeting after his grandmother's death, a boy finds that familiar songs, food and gathered people give him a sense of belonging.

passage:
The overnight train back from Grandpa's funeral rattled and clanked, and the compartment was full of snoring strangers. Zubin couldn't sleep. Where exactly was Grandpa now?
At dinner, Aunty Roshan had said, "He's with God, watching over you." His cousin Thomas, eating chips on the top berth, had said, "He's just gone, like switching off a light." Grandma said he would be born again. Zubin's head felt tangled.
He climbed down to where Dad sat by the window. "Dad, who's right?"
Dad thought for a long time while the stations flashed past. "People believe different things. Some believe what Aunty says, some what Grandma says. Honestly, nobody knows everything. You can keep asking, and decide what you believe slowly."
Zubin leaned against Dad's arm. The tangle didn't vanish, but it felt allowed.

qa.q: What did Thomas say about Grandpa?
qa.a: "He's just gone, like switching off a light."

qa.q: How did Zubin feel after hearing the different answers?
qa.a: Confused and unsettled; his head felt tangled.

qa.q: What made Dad's answer helpful?
qa.a: He was honest that people believe different things and nobody knows everything, and he said Zubin could keep asking.

qa.q: Why might each adult have answered Zubin differently?
qa.a: They each hold different beliefs about death, and each was probably trying to comfort Zubin in their own way.

grounding: A boy confused by different answers about where his grandfather has gone learns it is okay to ask and that nobody knows everything.

passage:
In their Ludhiana flat, Gurleen had drawn Dadaji four times that week: once as a star, once in a bright garden, once as a baby, once as just his empty chair.
"Why so many?" asked her big sister Jasleen.
"Because everybody says something different. Dadi says he's gone home to Waheguru. Harman at school says he's a star now. My science book says the heart just stops. Which one is true?"
Jasleen didn't answer. She took Gurleen to Mummy, who was folding Dadaji's turbans.
Mummy pulled Gurleen close. "Good question, puttar. Our family believes he has gone to Waheguru. Other families believe other things. Some things even grown-ups don't know for sure. You can ask me anything, any time."
Gurleen looked at her four drawings. Then she pinned them all on the wall, side by side.

qa.q: How many times had Gurleen drawn Dadaji that week?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen keep drawing Dadaji in different ways?
qa.a: She felt confused, because everyone told her something different about where he had gone.

qa.q: How did Mummy help with Gurleen's confusion?
qa.a: She shared the family's belief, said other families believe other things, admitted grown-ups do not know everything and invited any question.

qa.q: How might Jasleen have felt when she could not answer?
qa.a: Unsure herself, so she took Gurleen to Mummy.

grounding: A girl confused by the different answers about her grandfather's death is told that questions are welcome and that people hold different beliefs.

passage: Tarun, you think something is wrong with you because you didn't cry at your Nana's funeral? Listen to your Hansa Dadi. When I was about your age, my own grandfather died. Everyone wailed. I stood there feeling nothing, like a wooden doll. That night I lay awake thinking, am I a bad girl? Didn't I love him? In the morning I told my mother. She stroked my head and said, "Sadness comes to everybody in its own time." I went back to playing gilli-danda and felt guilty for playing. Three weeks later I found his spectacles in a drawer, and I cried so hard I couldn't stop. It had been waiting inside me. So play, Tarun. Cry when it comes. And tell me whenever it does.

qa.q: What did young Hansa find three weeks later?
qa.a: Her grandfather's spectacles in a drawer.

qa.q: What was young Hansa worried about after the funeral?
qa.a: She was worried and guilty, fearing she was a bad girl who didn't love him because she felt nothing.

qa.q: What choice in Dadi's story helped her?
qa.a: Telling her mother, who reassured her that sadness comes in its own time.

qa.q: How might Hansa's mother have seen her daughter's worry?
qa.a: She understood that children grieve in their own time and gently reassured her.

grounding: A grandmother recalls feeling nothing after a funeral and worrying about it, and how the grief came later once she had told a trusted adult.

passage:
Dadi's funeral was on Thursday, and the inter-school cricket final was on Saturday. Everyone expected Yash to skip it. But Yash felt nothing at all, just a flat grey quiet, so he went.
He hit two fours and even laughed when the ball smacked the umpire's shoe. Then, walking off, a horrible thought hit harder than any ball: what kind of grandson laughs two days after his Dadi dies?
He sat alone behind the pavilion. Coach Gautam Sir found him there. "You played well. What's wrong?"
Yash blurted it out. "I didn't cry. Now I'm laughing. I think I'm broken."
Gautam Sir sat beside him. "You're not broken. People grieve differently. Sometimes the tears come later, sometimes in small bits. Tell your parents what you told me, tonight. And if it comes during practice, you can sit out, no questions."
Yash nodded, and his shoulders came down a little.

qa.q: What did Yash hit in the final?
qa.a: Two fours.

qa.q: What was Yash worried about behind the pavilion?
qa.a: He felt guilty and scared that something was wrong with him because he felt nothing and even laughed.

qa.q: What did Gautam Sir advise?
qa.a: That Yash is not broken, people grieve differently, he should tell his parents tonight, and he can sit out practice if feelings come.

qa.q: How might Gautam Sir have seen Yash sitting alone?
qa.a: As a boy carrying a heavy worry after his Dadi's death, needing reassurance more than cricket talk.

grounding: A boy who feels nothing after his grandmother's funeral worries he is broken and learns from a trusted adult that grief comes in different ways and times.

passage:
Tuesday
First day back at school since Biji died. Everyone had something to say. "Don't cry, she's in a better place." "At least she was old." "You should keep busy." Each one made me feel worse, like I was doing grief wrong.
At lunch I sat on the back steps. Tanuja came and sat next to me. She didn't say anything. She just opened her tiffin and put half her aloo paratha on my lid. We sat there the whole break. Once I cried a bit, and she handed me her hanky and looked at the trees.
That was the best part of today. I didn't have to explain anything.
Tomorrow I'll sit with her again.
Amandeep

qa.q: What did Tanuja put on Amandeep's lid?
qa.a: Half her aloo paratha.

qa.q: How did the classmates' advice make Amandeep feel?
qa.a: Worse and misunderstood, as if Amandeep was grieving the wrong way.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja's quiet company help more than advice?
qa.a: She stayed close without asking Amandeep to explain or to feel differently.

qa.q: What might Tanuja have wanted when she looked at the trees?
qa.a: She probably wanted to give Amandeep some privacy while still staying close.

grounding: A child grieving a grandmother finds that a friend's quiet company helps more than advice.

passage:
Three days after Dadaji's cremation, Hrithik walked to the canal bank where they used to fish together. He sat on the flat rock and threw pebbles, one after another. Plop. Plop.
Nirmala from the next house saw him from the path. She came and sat on the other end of the rock. She didn't say "sorry" or "don't be sad". She just threw pebbles too.
After a long time Hrithik said, "He always caught more fish than me."
Nirmala nodded. "He gave my Ma fish sometimes."
They went quiet again. A heron landed. Hrithik's eyes filled, and Nirmala shifted a little closer so their shoulders touched.
When the sun went low, she stood up. "Same time tomorrow?"
"Same time," Hrithik said, and for the first time in days his chest didn't feel so tight.

qa.q: Where did Hrithik and Dadaji use to fish?
qa.a: At the canal bank.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's chest feeling less tight suggest?
qa.a: He felt comforted and less alone after Nirmala's quiet company.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do that helped?
qa.a: She sat with him, threw pebbles too and moved closer, without offering advice.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see the afternoon on the rock?
qa.a: As a way to care for a grieving friend just by being there; she even offered to come again.

grounding: A grieving boy is helped by a friend who sits quietly beside him, showing that being present is a strong way to care.

passage: Mohit, you said you feel sorry for the new boy with the torn chappals? Good heart. But let your Wasim Chacha tell you about a mistake I made. In Class 4 there was a boy, Ramu, whose shoes flapped open at the toe. I felt so sorry for him. So one morning I brought my old shoes in a bag and handed them to him in front of the whole class. "Here, you can have these." Everyone looked. Ramu went red, pushed the bag back and didn't speak to me for a week. I was hurt. I had meant well! My Abba explained, "You made him small in front of everyone." So I tried again, differently. I asked Ramu to join my kabaddi team. He turned out to be the best raider in school. We shared lunch, and later, quietly, other things too. Be his friend first, Mohit.

qa.q: What did young Wasim hand Ramu in front of the class?
qa.a: His old shoes in a bag.

qa.q: How did young Wasim feel when Ramu pushed the bag back?
qa.a: Hurt and confused, since he had meant well.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Chacha's story?
qa.a: Choosing to treat Ramu as an equal by asking him onto the kabaddi team, which made them friends.

qa.q: Why did Ramu push the bag back?
qa.a: Being handed shoes in front of everyone made him feel embarrassed and small.

grounding: An elder recalls how his pity for a poorer classmate made the boy feel small, and how friendship as equals worked instead.

passage:
The monsoon had flooded the school lane knee-deep, and the bus dropped everyone at the far corner. Arohi noticed Chinmay's canvas shoes, split along both sides, filling with muddy water at every step. He was pretending not to notice.
A tight feeling rose in her chest. Poor Chinmay, she thought, and the words almost came out loud in front of the others. She stopped herself. How would she feel if someone said that about her?
Instead she pulled two plastic bags from her raincoat pocket. "Mummy packed extra. Want to make boots? We'll both look ridiculous."
Chinmay hesitated, then grinned. They tied the bags over their shoes and waddled through the water like ducks, laughing so hard they were late for assembly.

qa.q: What did Arohi pull from her raincoat pocket?
qa.a: Two plastic bags.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when she saw Chinmay's shoes?
qa.a: She felt sorry for him, with a tight feeling in her chest.

qa.q: Why was Arohi's choice better than saying "Poor Chinmay"?
qa.a: Making silly boots together shared the help as equals instead of pointing out his torn shoes in front of others.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when Arohi offered the bags?
qa.a: At first hesitant and perhaps embarrassed, then relieved and happy, because they both looked silly together.

grounding: A girl who pities a classmate with torn shoes stops herself from saying it aloud and helps him as an equal.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Monday
After Lavanya's birthday party at her big bungalow on Saturday, Chetan was unusually quiet. During art he muttered, "She has a swimming pool and a games room. We have one room. I'm nothing next to her." He scribbled over his drawing.
At break I sat with him. I didn't tell him not to feel it; envy is a normal feeling. I asked him to list three things he is good at. He wrote: "fastest runner, can fix bicycles, makes my sister laugh."
Then something I hadn't planned: Lavanya, overhearing, said, "I wish I had a sister. My house is really quiet." Chetan looked at her in surprise.
They spent the rest of break racing. I will keep an eye on him this week.

qa.q: What three things did Chetan write that he is good at?
qa.a: Fastest runner, can fix bicycles, makes his sister laugh.

qa.q: What was Chetan feeling when he scribbled over his drawing?
qa.a: Envious and small, as if he was nothing next to Lavanya.

qa.q: How did the class teacher help Chetan?
qa.a: They accepted the feeling as normal and asked him to list three things he is good at.

qa.q: What did Lavanya's remark show Chetan?
qa.a: That she felt lonely in her quiet house, so having more money did not make her happier.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy envious of a wealthy classmate who is helped to see his own gifts and learns wealth does not make her happier.

passage:
Friday
Disha got dropped at school in a huge white car again, and she showed everyone her new tablet. I looked at my brother's old school bag with the broken zip and felt about two centimetres tall.
All day I kept thinking: her house, her car, her holidays. I didn't even enjoy the singing period, and singing is my favourite.
At night I told Nani. She didn't say "don't be jealous". She said, "Wanting things is normal. Now tell me what you have that no car can buy." I said my voice. She said my laugh. We argued about my handwriting (she says neat, I say messy).
Disha is nice, actually. Having more things doesn't make her better than me. It just means she has more things.
Rekha

qa.q: What did Disha show everyone?
qa.a: Her new tablet.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel looking at the old school bag?
qa.a: Small and envious, about two centimetres tall.

qa.q: How did Nani help Rekha with the envy?
qa.a: She accepted the feeling as normal and helped Rekha name gifts no car can buy, like Rekha's voice and laugh.

qa.q: What would change if Rekha kept comparing all the time?
qa.a: Rekha would keep missing joys like the singing period and might start resenting Disha, who is actually nice.

grounding: A child envious of a wealthier classmate talks to a grandparent, sees their own gifts and realises wealth does not make anyone better.
